name: Koreatown Run Club
who: Weekly Wednesday-night run through K-town, open to anyone who shows up, plus race-day meetups.
why: Grew from a handful of friends into one of LA's largest weekly run turnouts and a symbol of the 2020s run-club boom.
takeaway: Just show up any Wednesday night for the K-town run — open to anyone, plus race-day meetups.

name: Bridge Runners
who: NYC's original run crew, meeting Wednesdays since the mid-2000s; open group runs, no pace requirement.
why: Widely credited as the first modern run crew, the template every later crew copied.
takeaway: Show up Wednesdays in NYC — no pace requirement, just the city's original run crew since the 2000s.

name: Harlem Run
who: Free Monday/Tuesday/Wednesday runs through Harlem since 2013, plus a Thursday speed session; join by showing up.
why: One of the crews that pushed the 2010s NYC run-crew wave into a national health movement.
takeaway: Show up Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday for a free Harlem run, or Thursday for the speed session.

name: Black Men Run
who: National nonprofit with locally run weekly chapter runs across dozens of US cities; join via a city chapter.
why: Built a nationwide chapter network for Black men's health and running, filling a gap the big race brands didn't.
takeaway: Join a city chapter for locally run weekly chapter runs, part of a nationwide Black men's health network.

name: Black Girls RUN!
who: National running organization since 2009 with weekly run/walk meetups through dozens of city chapters.
why: One of the largest and longest-running Black women's fitness networks in the US, with charity marathon teams at Boston and Chicago.
takeaway: Find your city chapter for weekly run/walk meetups, or join their charity marathon teams at Boston or Chicago.

name: Slow AF Run Club
who: Paid online membership community for back-of-the-pack runners, founded by Martinus Evans; in-person meetups at races.
why: Built the largest inclusive back-of-the-pack running community by reframing slow running as its own identity, not a deficit.
takeaway: Join the paid online community for back-of-the-pack runners, then meet up in person at races.

name: November Project
who: Free outdoor workout movement born in Boston in 2011, mixing running and bodyweight training; no sign-up, just show up.
why: Boston's flagship chapter spawned free-workout chapters in dozens of cities and helped define pre-pandemic community fitness culture.
takeaway: No sign-up, just show up for free outdoor running and bodyweight training in Boston or beyond.

name: District Running Collective
who: Free Wednesday and Saturday urban run crew since 2013; hosts its own District 19 race series each October.
why: Built its own signature race and marathon-training program on top of a weekly free crew, rare for an independent group.
takeaway: Join the free Wednesday or Saturday urban run, or train for their own District 19 race each October.

name: Prospect Park Track Club
who: Traditional dues-paying club, 40-plus years old, with coached marathon training, speed work, and group runs around Prospect Park.
why: Brooklyn's largest and oldest running club, the traditional-club counterweight to the newer crew scene.
takeaway: Pay dues to join coached marathon training, speed work and group runs around Prospect Park.

name: San Francisco Road Runners Club
who: Dues-based club, 25-plus years old, with nearly 600 members and pace-grouped runs Tuesday through Sunday.
why: SF's largest and most historic road-running club, still running a full weekly calendar of coached sessions.
takeaway: Pay dues to join pace-grouped runs Tuesday through Sunday with SF's largest historic road-running club.

name: We Run Uptown
who: Washington Heights/Inwood crew running Monday (easy) and Wednesday (faster) since 2013; free and open.
why: Nike-backed but community-run, and one of the few crews to hold down a single uptown neighborhood for over a decade.
takeaway: Show up Monday for an easy run or Wednesday for a faster one in Washington Heights/Inwood — free and open.

name: Renegade Running
who: Run-specialty store and community founded 2020, running training programs, group runs, and an elite team from its Mandela Parkway shop.
why: Built a diverse Oakland running culture around a physical storefront and now fields an elite team coached by Nell Rojas.
takeaway: Drop into the Mandela Parkway shop for group runs, training programs, or watch the elite team train.

name: Boyle Heights Bridge Runners
who: Free Wednesday-night crew from Mariachi Plaza across the Sixth Street Bridge since 2013; all levels welcome.
why: A grassroots Eastside crew that drew national media (LA Times, Bourdain, Lisa Ling) for turning a run into neighborhood advocacy.
takeaway: Show up free Wednesday nights at Mariachi Plaza to cross the Sixth Street Bridge with the crew, all levels.

name: Run for Chinatown
who: Monday-night group run/walk from Columbus Park since 2021, started to bring foot traffic back to Manhattan's Chinatown.
why: A pandemic-recovery crew that turned into one of the clearest examples of running as neighborhood economic support.
takeaway: Show up Monday nights at Columbus Park for a group run/walk supporting Manhattan's Chinatown.

name: Lost Boys Track Club
who: Decentralized, competitive offshoot of Brooklyn Track Club chasing relay records (sub-2-hour marathon relays, Hood to Coast wins).
why: The performance edge of the NYC crew scene — a group of self-organized amateurs beating pro-adjacent relay times.
takeaway: Join this decentralized, competitive Brooklyn Track Club offshoot chasing relay records like sub-2-hour marathon relays.

name: Bakline
who: Brooklyn running and sportswear brand since 2008 that runs its own training groups and events alongside its gear line.
why: One of the earliest brand-run-club hybrids in NYC, blending street-culture design with an actual running community.
takeaway: Join this Brooklyn brand's own training groups and events alongside its running and sportswear gear line.

name: Old Man Run Club
who: Saturday-morning long-run crew founded by Public School's Dao-Yi Chow and Eugene Tong; Nike- and Oakley-backed, all paces.
why: A fashion-world crew that gave the run-club scene its long-run counterpart to weeknight speed sessions.
takeaway: Show up Saturday morning for the long run with this Nike- and Oakley-backed NYC crew, all paces.

name: Endorphins Running
who: New Balance-backed running community spanning nine US cities, running 2,000-plus free group runs a year plus a coaching app.
why: Scaled a single-city crew into a multi-city brand platform faster than almost any other US running community.
takeaway: Join one of 2,000-plus free group runs a year across nine US cities, or train with the app.

name: Midnight Runners
who: US chapter of the global Midnight Runners movement: runs mixed with music and bootcamp-style stops, volunteer-led.
why: Brought the UK-born run-and-party format to New York, leaning on social atmosphere over pace or mileage.
takeaway: Free to join in any of 18 cities — turn up for a night run that turns into a party.
